html:
The seizure of most white-owned commercial farms in Zimbabwe, begun in 2000 by the government of Robert Mugabe.

At independence in 1980 a few thousand white farmers still held much of the best land, a legacy of colonial Rhodesia. Land hunger had been a main cause of the Bush War. The Lancaster House Agreement that ended the war allowed land to change hands only from willing sellers, with Britain paying half the cost, and progress was slow. In the late 1990s British funding ended.

In 2000, after voters rejected a new constitution and a strong opposition party rose, war veterans and ruling party militants began occupying farms, and the government made it policy as "fast-track" reform. Owners and many farm workers were driven off, sometimes violently. Land went to small farmers but also to officials and their allies.

Commercial farming collapsed. Exports of tobacco and harvests of maize fell, food shortages followed, and the economy slid into hyperinflation. By 2013 almost all white-owned farms had been taken. Seizure without payment ended in 2018, after Mugabe's fall.
sum: The seizure of most white-owned commercial farms in Zimbabwe, begun in 2000 by the government of Robert Mugabe.
